note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SILKY FINGERS
tiles.details: Look at archived Australian panels 1 (source-identified living flowering tuft with roots hidden) and 4 (attached densely silky racemes and long dark awns). GrassBase describes about 1–6 racemes commonly 4–7 cm long, but broader floras and infraspecific forms overlap Kleberg. Australian photographs demonstrate habit, NOT a verified Texas subspecies or rooted local voucher. Do not rely on silvery color, raceme number or a bearded node alone.
tiles.short: Real silky racemes + dark awns photographed; actual Texas subspecies unverified
tiles.status: SOURCE AUTHENTIC HEAD/HABIT PHOTOS — TX SAME-VOUCHER ROOTED FORM MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · BEARDED NODE VS LIGULE
tiles.details: Actual source-labelled silky bluestem NODE hair-ring photograph (panel 0) clearly shows a white beard around the true upright stem joint; panel 2 is DIFFERENT introduced Kleberg bluestem with a similar bearded node. The newly presented local CC BY 2.0 leaf/sheath image (panel 3) instead shows the blade and cylindrical sheath on the stem. Its two new gross arrows do NOT mark the true INNER ligule. AusGrass describes an ECILIATE membranous ligule about 0.5–1 mm (VicFlora subsp. sericeum ~1–2 mm): photograph the actual free membrane edge with 1-mm ruler, separate from the MUCH LONGER nodal beard and side hairs. Never treat beard presence alone as species proof.
tiles.short: Hairy TRUE stem node is shared; inner ligule is a tiny membrane.
tiles.status: TRUE INNER LIGULE MEMBRANE NOW PHOTOGRAPHED (panel 5), still no 1-mm reference or local Texas voucher

tiles.heading: 03 · ROOTED TUFT AND RACEME INSERTION
tiles.details: The Australian whole-habit (panel 1, LOCALLY ARCHIVED) and local true sheath photo (panel 3) together support a bunching growth lesson, but NONE shows visibly exposed actual roots, crown-to-head physical continuity or possible short belowground rhizomes. Kew's broader descriptions call many perennial forms caespitose with occasional short rhizomes, while AusGrass distinguishes annual subsp. humilius from perennial subsp. sericeum. A Texas photographed individual could therefore differ in life cycle from the perennial Australian model. Rooted local same-voucher specimen, actual lower tiller connections and intact attached head required.
tiles.short: Australian tuft is context, not proof of Texas annual/perennial subspecies
tiles.status: IN-SITU BUNCHED HABIT PARTIAL; TRUE ROOTED CROWN AND TEXAS ID MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · TWO DIFFERENT SPIKELETS
tiles.details: In the actual licensed Australian head image (panel 4), densely silky flowering branches, visible long brown awns and spikelet-bearing rachis are source-authenticated. But the tiny individual sessile fertile spikelet and adjacent pedicelled sterile companion, plus 2–6 basal sterile pairs, cannot be independently measured from those pixels. AusGrass describes fertile sessile ~4–4.5 mm and sterile pedicelled ~3–5 mm (depending infraspecific treatment). The taxon must be dissected at 10–30× and photographed with a physical 1-mm scale; apparent strand/awn position alone is insufficient.
tiles.short: Measure a 4–4.5 mm sessile fertile spikelet beside a 3–5 mm pedicelled sterile one.
tiles.status: SOURCE-IDENTIFIED SPIKELET PAIR + SEPARATE SESSILE/PEDICELLED REAL SCALE PHOTOS ADDED

tiles.heading: 05 · GLUME FRINGE, LEMMAS AND AWN
tiles.details: This photographed head shows pale hairs and long stiff awns as broad morphology, but individual LOWER GLUME transverse subapical ciliary arch and BOTH glume surfaces are too small/hidden for true anatomical annotation. AusGrass keys subsp. humilius (~4-mm spikelet, 5–7-veined lower glume, often raceme shorter than 4 cm, annual) against subsp. sericeum (~4.5 mm, 9–10-veined, usually >4-cm raceme, perennial). These ranges are PUBLISHED, not yet demonstrated for any Texas voucher or the Australian photo. Isolate the actual sessile lower glume, its transverse hair line, attached awned fertile upper lemma, separate pedicelled sterile partner, and mm bar from the SAME specimen.
tiles.short: Find the lower glume's transverse hair fringe and one bent fertile-lemma awn.
tiles.status: REAL DISSECTED REPRODUCTIVE UNIT ADDED; EXACT FERTILE LEMMA/AWN ORIGIN STILL UNLABELLED

tiles.heading: 06 · DON'T CONFUSE SILKY, KLEBERG AND NATIVES
tiles.details: The five-panel lesson has FOUR source-identified silky-bluestem photographs: 0 (bearded true node), 1 (Australian living flowering tuft), 3 (blade/sheath; true inner ligule not exposed), and 4 (attached silky awned head). Panel 2 is explicitly DIFFERENT SPECIES Kleberg bluestem. The separately archived Melissa Walsh CC BY-NC original is not in this five-panel gallery. Both introduced Dichanthium species can have white-bearded nodes; KR and native cane bluestems also overlap in gross flowering appearance. Compare Texas rooted base, actual collar, complete raceme insertion and same-specimen mature sessile/pedicelled spikelet pair, lower-glume transverse subapical hair fringe and lemma awn origin. Preserve uncertain identifications and native look-alikes.
tiles.short: Photographs support node/sheath/head; no measured pair or certified Texas subspecies
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — NINE OPEN-LICENSE EXACT PHOTOS, ONE DIFFERENT-SPECIES COMPARISON, TX ROOTED CROWN STILL MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: SILKY BLUESTEM (introduced): LOOK HERE FIRST for a tight, densely white-silky cluster of terminal racemes, then trace the entire flowering culm to its base. A white-bearded TRUE STEM NODE is shared with Kleberg and some native bluestems, not proof of silky. Inspect an attached sessile fertile spikelet beside its pedicelled sterile companion, the lower glume's transverse subapical hair fringe and the fertile-lemma awn. Texas plants may differ from the photographed Australian forms; do not infer subspecies, native status or species ID from color or one detached head.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1 · HAIR RING: photo panel 0, actual hairy CULM NODE (Harry Rose CC BY 2.0 local file). The node beard is separate from the leaf collar. Panel 2 Kleberg also has a node beard!
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Actual source-labelled silky bluestem NODE hair-ring photograph (panel 0) clearly shows a white beard around the true upright stem joint; panel 2 is DIFFERENT introduced Kleberg bluestem with a similar bearded node. The newly presented local CC BY 2.0 leaf/sheath image (panel 3) instead shows the blade and cylindrical sheath on the stem. Its two new gross arrows do NOT mark the true INNER ligule. AusGrass describes an ECILIATE membranous ligule about 0.5–1 mm (VicFlora subsp. sericeum ~1–2 mm): photograph the actual free membrane edge with 1-mm ruler, separate from the MUCH LONGER nodal beard and side hairs. Never treat beard presence alone as species proof.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: The Australian whole-habit (panel 1, LOCALLY ARCHIVED) and local true sheath photo (panel 3) together support a bunching growth lesson, but NONE shows visibly exposed actual roots, crown-to-head physical continuity or possible short belowground rhizomes. Kew's broader descriptions call many perennial forms caespitose with occasional short rhizomes, while AusGrass distinguishes annual subsp. humilius from perennial subsp. sericeum. A Texas photographed individual could therefore differ in life cycle from the perennial Australian model. Rooted local same-voucher specimen, actual lower tiller connections and intact attached head required.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: White bearded culm nodes are SHARED with Kleberg and many native cane bluestems. Silky usually has densely villous relatively more sessile flowering racemes and a glume subapical ciliate fringe; Kleberg commonly more stalked subdigitate racemes, with basal sterile/unawned pairs. A mature source-verified spikelet pair and attached full head is the only secure species-level test when silhouettes overlap.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: Silky habit
panels.caption: See the relatively tight tuft carrying narrow hairy terminal raceme clusters. The view does NOT show species-level glume characters or hidden roots; growing context is Australian and should not imply this plant is native to Texas.

panels.label: SILKY ATTACHED RACEMES — actual long dark awns (LOCAL)
panels.caption: A real flowering head from New South Wales shows three tightly grouped silky flowering branches and separate long projecting brown awns. Silky hair is borne along the spikelet-bearing branches; the awns are longer and stiffer. This picture does NOT isolate the tiny sessile fertile vs pedicelled sterile spikelets or identify the transverse hair arch on a single lower glume. It is a CC BY 2.0 image now stored in GitHub with exact creator and source credits.

panels.label: ACTUAL INNER LIGULE — short pale membrane at the sheath mouth
panels.caption: Real source-identified Australian silky bluestem: the green sheath has been separated from its blade and a short pale, uneven-edged membranous ligule projects at the opening. The pointed white collar edge is NOT the long hairy culm-node beard. No real millimeter ruler accompanies this photo.

panels.label: REAL SPIKELET PAIR — long dark awn and white glume hairs
panels.caption: This is a real source-labelled silky bluestem spikelet-pair photograph, not a cropped whole seedhead. See overlapping green bracts, long pale hairs and a dark angled awn. The individual attachment of the pedicelled versus sessile units cannot safely be arrowed independently in this image.

panels.label: SESSILE SPIKELET — genuine individual structure beside a ruler
panels.caption: Source-identified fertile sessile spikelet from an Australian plant. The outer glume, shining green longitudinal ribs and hairy margins are visible beside actual dark graduated scale ticks. The original scale is not independently calibrated here; do not publish a measured 4-mm assertion from these pixels alone.

panels.label: PEDICELLED SPIKELET — matched companion close-up with ruler
panels.caption: The actual stalked companion, photographed independently by Harry Rose. It has a slightly different shape and fine hairs from the sessile fertile spikelet. The tick markings are physically in the source photo, but their numerical spacing must not be assumed.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)

panels.caption: A real microscopic dissection from Harry Rose with individual tiny pieces deliberately separated on the left and the hairy spikelet assembly on the right. The three pieces are NOT arrow-certified as specific glumes, lemmas or paleas because the source caption does not identify each boundary in this crop.

memory_rule: SILKY can have a conspicuous WHITE NODE BEARD TOO. Confirm attached racemes and glume hair fringe, not just the beard.
safety_note: Three physically archived original species images preserved (1 conditional CC BY-NC historical + 2 CC BY 2.0 originals); only two open-license local images featured in 5-panel gallery. New species-matched external head is CC BY 2.0 with exact source credit but NOT a local image. No individually exposed rooted crown, scaled ligule or measured lower-glume transverse cilia / fertile lemma awn insertion. User mobile arrow and live website validation pending.
field_rule: A long white stem-NODE beard belongs to both silky and Kleberg and is NOT the inner ligule. Real mature sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs and lower-glume transverse fringe separate taxa more meaningfully. A Texas subspecies cannot be certified from Australian photographic material.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
